q: The IUPAC name of the straight-chain alkane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is:
x: The chain has six carbon atoms joined by single bonds, so it is hexane. Pentane has five carbons and heptane seven.

q: A component of petrol has the condensed formula (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂CH₃. Following IUPAC rules, this compound is named:
x: The longest chain has five carbons, and numbering from the end nearer the branch puts the methyl group on carbon 2. 4-methylpentane numbers from the wrong end.

q: Number the longest chain in CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ so that the branches get the lowest locants. The resulting systematic name is:
x: The longest chain is five carbons, with methyl groups on carbons 2 and 3 when numbered from the left. Numbering from the right would give the higher locants 3,4.

q: Hexane and its chain isomers all share the formula C₆H₁₄. Including hexane itself, the total number of such isomers is:
x: They are hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane: five in all.

q: Removing a hydrogen from the middle carbon of propane gives the substituent (CH₃)₂CH–. Its common name is:
x: (CH₃)₂CH– has three carbons and is attached through the middle carbon, so it is isopropyl. n-propyl, CH₃CH₂CH₂–, is attached through an end carbon.

q: The name 2-ethylpropane is wrong. The structure it describes is correctly named:
x: 2-ethylpropane is CH₃CH(C₂H₅)CH₃, whose longest chain is four carbons with a methyl on carbon 2: 2-methylbutane. An ethyl group on carbon 2 always means a longer chain was missed.

q: When naming a branched alkane by the IUPAC system, the parent chain chosen is:
o: The longest continuous chain of carbon atoms
The chain with the most branches written on the left
Any chain that is written in a straight line
The shortest chain that contains all the branches
x: The parent name comes from the longest continuous carbon chain, however it is drawn. Branches are then numbered from the end that gives them the lowest locants.

q: Choosing the six-carbon parent chain of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃ and numbering it correctly gives the systematic name:
x: The longest chain has six carbons. Numbering from the right end puts the methyl groups on carbons 2 and 4, lower than 3 and 5 from the left.

q: Which of the following species is a free radical?
x: Cl• is a neutral chlorine atom with one unpaired electron. Cl⁻ and Cl⁺ are ions, and Cl₂ is a molecule with all electrons paired.

q: Which equation is the first propagation step in the chlorination of methane?
x: In propagation a radical reacts with a molecule to give a new radical: Cl• removes H from CH₄, forming HCl and CH₃•. Splitting Cl₂ is initiation; the radical–radical steps are termination.

q: How many electrons are present in the outer shell of a chlorine free radical, Cl•?
x: A chlorine atom has 7 outer electrons, one of them unpaired. Gaining an eighth electron would make it the chloride ion, Cl⁻, which is not a radical.

q: Which type of bond breaking produces ions rather than free radicals?
o: Homolytic fission, where each atom takes one bonding electron
Heterolytic fission, where one atom takes both bonding electrons
Homolytic fission, where neither atom takes an electron
Heterolytic fission, where each atom takes one bonding electron
x: In heterolytic fission both shared electrons go to one atom, giving a positive and a negative ion. Homolytic fission shares the electrons equally and gives free radicals.

q: Free radicals are very reactive because:
o: They carry a large positive charge
They have a complete octet of electrons
They have an unpaired electron that tends to pair up by forming a bond
They are always very heavy species
x: The unpaired electron makes a radical unstable, so it reacts quickly to gain a partner electron. Radicals are neutral and do not have a complete octet.

q: Which of the following is NOT a termination step in the chlorination of methane?
x: Termination removes radicals by joining two of them. CH₃• + Cl₂ produces a new radical, Cl•, so it is a propagation step.

q: In the chlorination of ethane, which two species can combine in a termination step to give chloroethane?
x: An ethyl radical joining a chlorine radical gives C₂H₅Cl. Two ethyl radicals give butane, two chlorine radicals give Cl₂, and two methyl radicals give ethane.

q: Which statement about the number of free radicals in each stage of a free-radical chain reaction is correct?
o: Initiation decreases it, propagation increases it, termination keeps it constant
All three stages increase the number of radicals
Initiation increases it, propagation keeps it constant, termination decreases it
Initiation and termination both increase it, while propagation decreases it
x: Initiation splits a molecule into two radicals; each propagation step uses one radical and makes one; termination joins two radicals into a molecule.

q: Methane is treated with a limited amount of bromine in sunlight. The main products are:
x: Bromination follows the same free-radical substitution as chlorination: CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr. With little bromine, mainly one hydrogen is replaced.

q: Fluoromethane is not made by mixing methane directly with fluorine because:
o: Fluorine does not react with methane at all
The reaction needs a nickel catalyst
The reaction is explosive and hard to control
Fluorine adds to methane instead of substituting
x: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen, and its reaction with methane is violent, even explosive. Methane has no multiple bond, so addition is not possible.

q: Ethane is chlorinated further, giving products with molecular formula C₂H₃Cl₃. Counting different positional arrangements of chlorine, these products exist as how many isomers?
x: The three chlorines can all be on one carbon (1,1,1-trichloroethane) or two on one carbon and one on the other (1,1,2-trichloroethane). No other arrangement is possible.

q: When three hydrogen atoms of methane are replaced by chlorine, the product is:
x: Replacing three H atoms of CH₄ gives CHCl₃, trichloromethane, commonly called chloroform. CCl₄ results when all four are replaced.

q: What volume of chlorine at STP is needed to convert 0.1 mol of methane completely into dichloromethane?
x: CH₄ + 2Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + 2HCl, so 0.1 mol CH₄ needs 0.2 mol Cl₂; 0.2 × 22.4 = 4.48 dm³. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives the wrong 2.24 dm³.

q: One mole of ethane is chlorinated until all its hydrogen atoms are replaced, giving C₂Cl₆. How many moles of HCl are formed?
x: C₂H₆ + 6Cl₂ → C₂Cl₆ + 6HCl: each hydrogen replaced produces one HCl. Ethane has six hydrogens, so 6 mol HCl.

q: Free-radical chlorination of methane usually gives a mixture of products because:
o: Methane contains carbon atoms of different types
Chlorine radicals add to methane at several positions
Some methane always changes into ethene first
The chloromethane formed can itself react with chlorine radicals
x: CH₃Cl still has C–H bonds, so Cl• can attack it to give CH₂Cl₂, then CHCl₃ and CCl₄. All four hydrogens in methane are equivalent, and no addition takes place.

q: During further chlorination of chloromethane, a chlorine radical removes a hydrogen atom from CH₃Cl. The radical formed is:
x: Cl• + CH₃Cl → •CH₂Cl + HCl. This radical then reacts with Cl₂ to give CH₂Cl₂ and a new Cl•.

q: Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, is heated with excess concentrated H₂SO₄. The alkene formed is:
x: Dehydration removes H₂O from the alcohol, leaving a C=C bond in the same three-carbon chain: CH₃CH=CH₂, propene.

q: 1-chlorobutane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Cl, is heated with alcoholic KOH. The organic product is:
x: Alcoholic KOH removes HCl from the carbon carrying Cl and its neighbour, giving CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂. Aqueous KOH would give the alcohol instead.

q: In the preparation of ethene from ethanol, concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as:
o: A dehydrating agent that removes water
An oxidising agent that removes hydrogen
A reducing agent that adds hydrogen
A source of sulphur for the product
x: Concentrated H₂SO₄ removes a water molecule from ethanol, leaving the C=C bond of ethene. No oxidation or reduction of the carbon chain occurs.

q: 2-bromobutane, CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃, is heated with alcoholic KOH. The major product is:
x: H can be lost from either neighbouring carbon, but the more substituted alkene, but-2-ene, is the major product. Butan-2-ol would form with aqueous KOH.

q: Which alkyl halide can NOT give an alkene by dehydrohalogenation?
x: Elimination needs a hydrogen on the carbon next to the one carrying the halogen. CH₃Cl has only one carbon, so there is no such hydrogen and no alkene can form.

q: When bromoethane is heated with alcoholic KOH to give ethene, the other products are:
x: CH₃CH₂Br + KOH → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O. The H and Br removed from the alkyl halide end up as water and potassium bromide.

q: 21.8 g of bromoethane, C₂H₅Br (M = 109), is completely converted into ethene by alcoholic KOH. What mass of ethene is formed? (C 12, H 1)
x: Moles of C₂H₅Br = 21.8/109 = 0.2 mol, giving 0.2 mol C₂H₄; 0.2 × 28 = 5.6 g.

q: The simplest alkene after ethene, CH₃CH=CH₂, has the IUPAC name:
x: A three-carbon chain with one C=C bond is propene. Numbering from the end nearer the double bond gives 1, so no locant is needed; prop-2-ene numbers from the wrong end.

q: An alkene with a branch next to its CH₂= end, CH₂=CHCH(CH₃)CH₃, is given which systematic name?
x: The chain is numbered from the end nearer the double bond, so C=C is at carbon 1 and the methyl group at carbon 3: 3-methylbut-1-ene.

q: One of the pentene isomers has the structure CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)=CH₂. Its systematic name is:
x: The longest chain containing the double bond has four carbons. Numbering from the CH₂= end puts C=C at carbon 1 and the methyl at carbon 2.

q: A symmetrical six-carbon alkene, CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₂CH₃, is named by IUPAC as:
x: The six-carbon chain has its double bond between carbons 3 and 4 from either end, so it is hex-3-ene.

q: The name pent-4-ene is incorrect. The correct IUPAC name of this compound is:
x: pent-4-ene numbers the chain from the wrong end. Numbering from the end nearer the double bond gives it the locant 1: pent-1-ene.

q: Pent-1-ene is one of several non-cyclic alkenes with five carbons and ten hydrogens. Ignoring cis–trans forms, the total number of such alkenes is:
x: They are pent-1-ene, pent-2-ene, 2-methylbut-1-ene, 3-methylbut-1-ene and 2-methylbut-2-ene: five structural isomers.

q: CH₂=CHCl is commonly called vinyl chloride. Its IUPAC name is:
x: It is ethene with one H replaced by Cl, so it is chloroethene. Chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl, has no double bond.

q: A student writes 2-ethylbut-2-ene as the name of CH₃CH=C(CH₂CH₃)CH₃. The correct systematic name is:
x: The longest chain through the double bond includes the ethyl group, giving five carbons, not four. Numbered from the left, C=C is at carbon 2 and the methyl at carbon 3.

q: Head-on overlap forming the C–C σ bond in ethene involves which orbitals?
x: Each carbon in ethene is sp² hybridised, and head-on overlap of one sp² orbital from each carbon forms the C–C σ bond. The unhybridised 2p orbitals form the π bond.

q: Free rotation about the C=C bond in ethene is not possible because:
o: The σ bond between the carbons is too short
The hydrogen atoms repel each other strongly
The carbon atoms are sp³ hybridised
Rotation would destroy the sideways overlap of the p orbitals forming the π bond
x: The π bond needs the two p orbitals to stay parallel. Twisting one carbon relative to the other would break this overlap, so rotation is restricted.

q: Counting single and double bonds in CH₂=CH₂, ethene contains:
x: There are four C–H σ bonds and one C–C σ bond, making 5 σ, plus one π bond in the double bond.

q: The C=C bond length in ethene is about:
x: The C=C bond in ethene is about 1.34 Å, shorter than the C–C bond in ethane (1.54 Å) and longer than the C≡C bond in ethyne (1.20 Å).

q: How many σ and π bonds are present in buta-1,3-diene, CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂?
x: There are six C–H σ bonds and three C–C σ bonds, making 9 σ. Each of the two double bonds also contains one π bond, giving 2 π.

q: For bonding, an ethene carbon has available:
o: Three sp² hybrid orbitals and one unhybridised p orbital
Two sp hybrid orbitals and two unhybridised p orbitals
Three sp² hybrid orbitals and no unhybridised p orbital
x: Mixing one 2s and two 2p orbitals gives three sp² orbitals for the σ bonds. The remaining 2p orbital on each carbon forms the π bond.

q: But-2-ene exists as separate cis and trans forms, but butane does not. This is because:
o: But-2-ene has more carbon atoms than butane
Butane has a π bond that can rotate freely
The carbons of but-2-ene are sp³ hybridised
Rotation about the C=C double bond is restricted
x: Restricted rotation about C=C fixes groups on the same side or opposite sides, giving geometric (cis–trans) isomers. In butane, rotation about the C–C σ bonds is free.

q: In propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃, the hybridisation of the carbons from the CH₂ end to the CH₃ end is:
x: Both carbons of the double bond are sp², while the CH₃ carbon has four single bonds and is sp³.

q: Ethene reacts with hydrogen bromide. The product is:
x: HBr adds across the double bond: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br. 1,2-dibromoethane forms with Br₂, not HBr.

q: Ethene is passed into chlorine water (containing HOCl). The organic product is:
x: HOCl adds across the double bond, putting Cl on one carbon and OH on the other: ClCH₂CH₂OH, ethylene chlorohydrin.

q: A few drops of cold, dilute alkaline KMnO₄ are added to a gas jar of ethene and shaken. What is seen?
o: The purple colour disappears and a brown precipitate forms
A white precipitate forms and the solution stays purple
The solution turns from orange to green
x: Ethene reduces MnO₄⁻, so the purple colour fades and brown MnO₂ appears, while ethene is oxidised to the diol. Orange to green is the change for dichromate.

q: Propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, is treated with ozone and the ozonide is broken down with zinc and water. The products are:
x: Ozonolysis splits the C=C bond and each carbon becomes C=O: CH₃CH= gives CH₃CHO (ethanal) and =CH₂ gives HCHO (methanal).

q: To saturate 14 g of ethene fully with H₂ over nickel, the mass of hydrogen required is: (C 12, H 1)
x: 14 g of C₂H₄ is 14/28 = 0.5 mol, which needs 0.5 mol H₂. 0.5 × 2 = 1 g.

q: In the electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene, the intermediate formed after the first step is:
x: H⁺ attaches to one carbon of the double bond, leaving a positive charge on the other: CH₃CH₂⁺. Br⁻ then joins this carbocation.

q: Which reagent distinguishes ethene from ethane at room temperature?
x: Ethene adds bromine and decolourises orange bromine water quickly; ethane, a saturated alkane, does not react in the dark.

q: An alkene C₄H₈ gives propanone (CH₃COCH₃) and methanal on ozonolysis followed by Zn/H₂O. The alkene is:
x: Joining the two carbonyl carbons with a C=C gives (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, 2-methylpropene. But-1-ene would give propanal and methanal, and but-2-ene only ethanal.

q: How many σ bonds are present in one molecule of benzene, C₆H₆?
x: Benzene has six C–C σ bonds in the ring and six C–H σ bonds, a total of 12. The π electrons are delocalised over the ring.

q: The carbon–carbon bond length in benzene is about:
x: All C–C bonds in benzene are about 1.39 Å, between the single-bond length (1.54 Å) and the double-bond length (1.34 Å). 1.20 Å is the C≡C length.

q: Kekulé proposed a ring of alternate single and double bonds for benzene. Which fact about benzene does this structure fail to explain?
o: Benzene has the molecular formula C₆H₆
Benzene does not readily undergo addition reactions as alkenes do
Benzene contains six carbon atoms in a ring
Benzene burns to give carbon dioxide and water
x: Three localised C=C bonds should make benzene add bromine as alkenes do, but it does not. The formula and ring are consistent with Kekulé's structure.

q: Benzene, C₆H₆, has the same empirical formula as:
x: Both C₆H₆ and C₂H₂ reduce to the empirical formula CH. Ethene and cyclohexane reduce to CH₂.

q: The C–C σ bonds that hold the benzene ring together are formed by overlap of:
o: sp² orbitals of neighbouring carbon atoms
Unhybridised p orbitals of neighbouring carbon atoms
sp³ orbitals of neighbouring carbon atoms
sp orbitals of neighbouring carbon atoms
x: Each ring carbon is sp² hybridised and uses two sp² orbitals for head-on overlap with its two neighbours. The unhybridised p orbitals form the delocalised π system.

q: In the molecular orbital treatment of benzene, the six p orbitals combine to form six π molecular orbitals. In the ground state, the six π electrons occupy:
o: All six molecular orbitals, one electron each
x: Six p orbitals give three bonding and three antibonding π orbitals. The six π electrons fill the three bonding orbitals in pairs, which makes benzene very stable.

q: Benzene is often drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside. The circle represents:
o: Six π electrons delocalised over all six carbon atoms
A ring of six hydrogen atoms
Six lone pairs on the carbon atoms
x: The circle shows that the π electrons are not fixed in three double bonds but spread evenly round the ring. Benzene has no lone pairs on carbon.

q: Which statement about the structure of benzene is NOT correct?
o: Each carbon atom is sp² hybridised
All twelve atoms lie in one plane
Each bond angle in the ring is 120°
It contains three short C=C bonds and three long C–C bonds
x: All six C–C bonds in benzene have the same length, 1.39 Å, because the π electrons are delocalised. The other statements are correct.

q: How many Kekulé structures are used to show resonance in benzene?
x: Benzene is shown as a resonance hybrid of two Kekulé structures, which differ only in where the three double bonds are placed.

q: Which pair of structures are resonance (contributing) structures?
o: The two Kekulé structures of benzene
x: The Kekulé structures have the same atom positions and differ only in where the π electrons are. Ethanol and dimethyl ether are structural isomers; cis and trans forms are geometric isomers.

q: All contributing structures of a molecule must have the same:
x: Resonance structures keep every atom in the same place and differ only in electron positions. The real hybrid has lower energy than any of them.

q: Which statement about the individual Kekulé structures of benzene is correct?
o: Each can be isolated at low temperature
They change into each other rapidly like two isomers
One is more stable and makes up most of a benzene sample
Neither exists on its own, so neither can be isolated
x: Contributing structures are only ways of writing the electrons. The real benzene molecule is a single hybrid; the two Kekulé structures are equivalent and neither exists separately.

q: The double-headed arrow (↔) written between the two Kekulé structures of benzene shows that:
o: The two structures are in a rapid chemical equilibrium
They are contributing structures of one hybrid, not two substances in equilibrium
One structure is converted completely into the other
The molecule vibrates between two shapes
x: ↔ means resonance: the real molecule is one structure intermediate between those drawn. An equilibrium between two real substances is shown by ⇌.

q: Which general statement about resonance and stability is correct?
o: A molecule with more contributing structures is always less stable
A molecule with more equivalent contributing structures generally gains more resonance stabilisation
Resonance makes a molecule higher in energy than its contributing structures
Resonance stabilisation is possible only for ions, not molecules
x: Spreading electrons over more equivalent structures lowers the energy of the hybrid, increasing stability. Resonance occurs in molecules such as benzene as well as in ions.

q: Applying the same idea used for benzene, the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻, has three equivalent contributing structures, each with one C=O and two C–O bonds. The bond order of each C–O bond in the hybrid is about:
x: Four bonding pairs (one double and two single bonds) are shared equally over three C–O bonds: 4/3 ≈ 1.33. Benzene's bond order of 1.5 comes from two structures, not three.

q: The measured enthalpy of combustion of benzene is less negative than the value calculated for a cyclohexatriene structure with three localised double bonds. This is evidence that benzene:
o: Is less stable than the Kekulé structure
Contains fewer hydrogen atoms than expected
x: Less heat released means the real molecule started at lower energy than the Kekulé model predicts. The difference is the resonance energy.

q: Towards addition reactions, benzene compared with ethene is:
x: Ethene adds bromine and hydrogen halides easily at room temperature. Benzene adds only under harsh conditions, because addition would destroy its stable delocalised π system.

q: Which reaction takes place with benzene but NOT with hexane?
o: Nitration with concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ at 50–55 °C
Complete combustion in air to give CO₂ and H₂O
Reaction with chlorine in ultraviolet light
x: Benzene's π electrons attract the NO₂⁺ electrophile, so it is nitrated under mild conditions; hexane has no π electrons and is not. Both burn and both react with Cl₂ in UV light, and neither decolourises cold KMnO₄.

q: Cyclohexene and benzene are each hydrogenated over a nickel catalyst. Which statement is correct?
o: Cyclohexene needs more severe conditions than benzene
Both react with hydrogen at room temperature without a catalyst
Benzene needs more severe conditions (higher temperature and pressure) than cyclohexene
x: The localised C=C bond of cyclohexene is hydrogenated easily. Benzene's resonance-stabilised ring resists addition, so higher temperature and pressure are needed.

q: Alkanes are generally unreactive towards acids, bases and oxidising agents because:
o: Their carbon atoms are sp² hybridised
Their carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen bonds are strong and almost non-polar, and they have no π electrons
They have lone pairs that repel reagents
x: With strong, nearly non-polar σ bonds and no π electrons, alkanes offer no site for polar reagents to attack. They react mainly by free-radical substitution.

q: Hex-1-ene, hexane and benzene are each shaken with cold, dilute alkaline KMnO₄. The purple colour disappears with:
x: Only an alkene with a localised C=C bond is oxidised by Baeyer's reagent to a diol. Benzene and hexane leave the purple colour unchanged.

q: Ethene reacts with bromine by electrophilic addition, and benzene reacts with bromine (with FeBr₃) by electrophilic substitution. In both reactions:
o: An electrophile attacks the π electrons of the hydrocarbon
A nucleophile attacks a carbon atom
Free radicals are formed by light
A hydrogen atom is first removed by a base
x: The π electrons of ethene and of benzene act as an electron source, so both are attacked by electrophiles. They differ only in what happens to the intermediate.

q: Rank hex-1-ene, benzene and hexane by how readily each is attacked by electrophiles.
x: The localised π electrons of hex-1-ene are most available. Benzene's delocalised π electrons react only with strong electrophiles and a catalyst. Hexane has no π electrons and does not react with electrophiles.

q: The molecular formula of benzene hexachloride (BHC) is:
x: Three molecules of Cl₂ add across the benzene ring without removing any hydrogen: C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₆Cl₆.

q: When ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, adds three moles of H₂ over Ni, the compound formed is:
x: Hydrogen adds to the ring (3 mol H₂ per mole) while the ethyl side chain is already saturated, giving ethylcyclohexane, C₆H₁₁CH₂CH₃.

q: 9.2 g of methylbenzene (C₇H₈, M = 92 g mol⁻¹) is hydrogenated completely to methylcyclohexane. What volume of hydrogen at STP is used?
x: Moles of methylbenzene = 9.2/92 = 0.1. It needs 3 mol H₂ per mole, so 0.3 mol × 22.4 = 6.72 dm³.

q: The addition of chlorine to benzene in bright sunlight takes place by:
x: Sunlight splits Cl₂ into chlorine free radicals, which add to the ring. With FeCl₃ in the dark the reaction would instead be electrophilic substitution.

q: Benzene is converted into cyclohexane by:
o: Heating with hydrogen in the presence of finely divided nickel
Shaking with hydrogen at room temperature without a catalyst
x: Catalytic hydrogenation needs a metal catalyst such as Ni (or Pt, Pd) and heat, because the stable aromatic ring resists addition.

q: 7.8 g of benzene is converted completely into benzene hexachloride, C₆H₆Cl₆ (M = 291 g mol⁻¹). What mass of product is formed? (C 12, H 1)
x: Moles of benzene = 7.8/78 = 0.1. One mole of benzene gives one mole of C₆H₆Cl₆, so mass = 0.1 × 291 = 29.1 g.

q: 0.2 mol of benzene adds chlorine completely in sunlight. What volume of chlorine at STP is used?
x: C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₆Cl₆, so 0.2 mol benzene needs 0.6 mol Cl₂; 0.6 × 22.4 = 13.44 dm³. 4.48 dm³ ignores the 1 : 3 ratio.

q: In the bromination of benzene with Br₂ and FeBr₃, the electrophile that attacks the ring is:
x: FeBr₃ polarises Br₂ and takes Br⁻ to form FeBr₄⁻, releasing the electrophile Br⁺, which attacks the π electrons of the ring.

q: In the arenium ion formed during electrophilic substitution, how many π electrons remain delocalised, and over how many carbon atoms?
x: Two of benzene's six π electrons form the new bond to the electrophile, and that carbon becomes sp³. The remaining 4 π electrons and the positive charge are spread over the other 5 carbons.

q: Which step restores the aromatic character of the ring in electrophilic substitution?
o: Formation of the electrophile from the reagent and catalyst
Attack of the electrophile on the π electrons
Addition of a nucleophile to the arenium ion
Loss of H⁺ from the arenium ion
x: When the sp³ carbon loses its H⁺, the two electrons of the C–H bond return to the ring, which regains its six delocalised π electrons.

q: Which equation shows how the electrophile is produced in the chlorination of benzene with FeCl₃?
x: The Lewis acid FeCl₃ accepts a chloride ion from Cl₂, leaving the chloronium electrophile Cl⁺. Splitting Cl₂ into radicals happens only in light.

q: When an electrophile E⁺ bonds to the benzene ring, the electrons used to form the new C–E bond come from:
o: The π electron cloud of the ring
A C–H bond of the ring
A lone pair on the electrophile
x: The benzene ring acts as an electron-pair donor: two of its π electrons form the new σ bond to E⁺, giving the arenium ion.

q: At the end of the bromination of benzene with Br₂ and FeBr₃, the FeBr₃:
o: Is used up and turned into iron metal
Is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst
x: FeBr₄⁻ removes H⁺ from the arenium ion, giving HBr and FeBr₃ again. Since it is not used up, FeBr₃ is a catalyst.

q: Which of the following species is NOT an electrophile?
x: NH₃ has a lone pair to donate, so it is a nucleophile. NO₂⁺, Cl⁺ and SO₃ are electron-seeking species that attack the benzene ring.

q: The organic product of the sulphonation of benzene is:
x: Benzene reacts with fuming H₂SO₄ to replace one H atom by –SO₃H, giving benzenesulphonic acid.

q: In the nitrating mixture, the role of concentrated sulphuric acid is to:
o: Act as the electrophile that attacks benzene
Supply sulphur that enters the ring
Protonate nitric acid so that it forms the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺
Reduce nitric acid to nitrogen dioxide
x: H₂SO₄ is the stronger acid; it protonates HNO₃, which then loses water to give NO₂⁺: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻.

q: In the Friedel–Crafts alkylation of benzene with chloromethane and AlCl₃, the electrophile is:
x: AlCl₃ removes Cl⁻ from CH₃Cl to form AlCl₄⁻ and the methyl carbocation CH₃⁺, which attacks the ring.

q: Benzene reacts with chloroethane, C₂H₅Cl, in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The organic product is:
x: This is Friedel–Crafts alkylation: an ethyl group replaces one ring H, giving C₆H₅C₂H₅ and HCl.

q: Benzene is treated with chlorine in the presence of anhydrous FeCl₃ in the dark. The products are:
x: With a Lewis acid catalyst and no light, chlorine substitutes one ring H: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ → C₆H₅Cl + HCl. Addition to give BHC needs sunlight and no catalyst.

q: 15.6 g of benzene is brominated with Br₂/FeBr₃ to give bromobenzene, C₆H₅Br. What mass of bromobenzene is formed if the yield is 100%? (C 12, H 1, Br 80)
x: Moles of benzene = 15.6/78 = 0.2. M(C₆H₅Br) = 72 + 5 + 80 = 157, so mass = 0.2 × 157 = 31.4 g. 32.0 g is the mass of Br₂ used.

q: The AlCl₃ used in Friedel–Crafts reactions must be anhydrous because:
o: Water reacts with benzene to form phenol
Anhydrous AlCl₃ is the electrophile that enters the ring
Water reacts with AlCl₃ so that it can no longer act as a Lewis acid catalyst
Water would make the reaction explosive
x: AlCl₃ is hydrolysed by water, losing its ability to accept a pair of electrons. It then cannot generate the carbocation or acylium ion.

q: An –OH group attached to a benzene ring is:
x: The –OH group donates electron density to the ring, making it more reactive and directing incoming electrophiles to the 2 and 4 positions.

q: Nitrobenzene is sulphonated with fuming sulphuric acid. The main product is:
x: The –NO₂ group is a meta-director, so the –SO₃H group enters position 3.

q: Ethylbenzene is treated with chlorine in the presence of FeCl₃ in the dark. The main products are:
x: An alkyl group is ortho/para-directing, and the Lewis acid catalyst gives ring substitution. Side-chain chlorination would need sunlight instead.

q: The –CHO group in benzaldehyde directs an incoming electrophile mainly to the:
x: –CHO withdraws electrons from the ring (like –COOH and –NO₂), so it deactivates the ring and is meta-directing.

q: Phenol, C₆H₅OH, undergoes electrophilic substitution much faster than benzene because the –OH group:
o: Withdraws electron density from the ring
Removes the π electrons from the ring
Makes the ring carbons sp³ hybridised
Donates electron density to the ring
x: The lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring, raising its electron density and making it more attractive to electrophiles.

q: Which sequence converts methylbenzene mainly into 4-nitrobenzoic acid?
o: Oxidise with hot KMnO₄ first, then nitrate
Nitrate first, then oxidise the side chain with hot KMnO₄
x: –CH₃ is ortho/para-directing, so nitration gives 4-nitromethylbenzene (plus the 2-isomer); oxidation then turns –CH₃ into –COOH. Oxidising first gives –COOH, a meta-director, leading to 3-nitrobenzoic acid.

q: Benzene is converted into acetophenone (C₆H₅COCH₃) by Friedel–Crafts acylation, and the product is then nitrated. The main nitration product is:
x: The –COCH₃ group withdraws electrons from the ring, so it is meta-directing and the –NO₂ group enters position 3.

q: Acetylene, HC≡CH, is the simplest alkyne. Its IUPAC name is:
x: The two-carbon chain is "eth-" and the triple bond gives the ending "-yne". Acetylene is its common name.

q: A straight-chain alkyne with five carbons has the structure CH₃C≡CCH₂CH₃. Its IUPAC name is:
x: The chain has five carbons. Numbering from the end nearer the triple bond puts it between C2 and C3, so the name is pent-2-yne, not pent-3-yne.

q: Name this branched alkyne by the IUPAC system: HC≡C–CH₂–CH(CH₃)₂
x: The longest chain containing the triple bond has five carbons. Numbering from the ≡CH end gives the triple bond position 1 and the methyl group position 4.

q: Which IUPAC name fits the alkyne CH₃–C≡C–C(CH₃)₃, which carries a tert-butyl group?
x: The longest chain through the triple bond has five carbons. Numbering from the CH₃ end next to the triple bond gives the triple bond position 2 and both methyls position 4.

q: Which condensed formula represents hex-3-yne?
x: Hex-3-yne has six carbons with the triple bond between C3 and C4, which is in the middle of the chain. The last formula is an alkene.

q: How many open-chain alkynes have the molecular formula C₄H₆?
x: Only but-1-yne (CH≡CCH₂CH₃) and but-2-yne (CH₃C≡CCH₃) are possible; a four-carbon chain with a triple bond cannot branch.

q: An alkyne has two isopropyl groups joined to the carbons of a triple bond, (CH₃)₂CH–C≡C–CH(CH₃)₂. Its IUPAC name is:
x: The longest chain through the triple bond has six carbons, with the triple bond at C3. The methyl branches are on C2 and C5 from either end.

q: A geminal dihalide is a compound in which:
o: The two halogen atoms are on neighbouring carbon atoms
The two halogen atoms are at opposite ends of the chain
Both halogen atoms are on the same carbon atom
The halogen atoms are on a benzene ring
x: Geminal (gem-) dihalides have both halogens on one carbon, e.g. CH₃CHBr₂. Vicinal (vic-) dihalides have them on adjacent carbons.

q: 1,2-dibromobutane, CH₂BrCHBrCH₂CH₃, is heated with alcoholic KOH and then treated with sodamide (NaNH₂). The main organic product is:
x: Two molecules of HBr are eliminated from the neighbouring carbons C1 and C2, so the triple bond forms between them, giving CH≡CCH₂CH₃.

q: When a vicinal dihalide is converted into an alkyne by dehydrohalogenation, the number of molecules of hydrogen halide removed from each molecule is:
x: Each elimination removes one HX and forms one π bond. Two eliminations convert the single C–C bond into a triple bond.

q: 2,2,3,3-tetrabromobutane, CH₃CBr₂CBr₂CH₃, is heated with zinc dust. The organic product is:
x: Zinc removes all four bromine atoms (as ZnBr₂) from the two central carbons, leaving a triple bond between C2 and C3.

q: 37.6 g of 1,2-dibromoethane (M = 188 g mol⁻¹) is converted completely into ethyne. What mass of ethyne is formed? (C 12, H 1)
x: Moles = 37.6/188 = 0.2. One mole of dibromide gives one mole of C₂H₂ (M = 26), so mass = 0.2 × 26 = 5.2 g.

q: Converting 1,2-dibromoethane into ethyne needs two eliminations. What happens to the hybridisation of the carbons?
x: The dibromide has only single bonds (sp³). The first elimination gives bromoethene with a double bond (sp²); the second gives the triple bond of ethyne (sp).

q: 1,2-dibromoethane is warmed with zinc dust (instead of being heated with alcoholic KOH). The organic product is:
x: Zinc removes the two bromine atoms from adjacent carbons (dehalogenation), forming only one π bond, so ethene is formed. Ethyne by this method needs a tetrahalide.

q: Which hydrocarbon reacts with sodium metal to give hydrogen gas?
x: Only the ≡C–H hydrogen of ethyne is acidic enough to be replaced by sodium, forming sodium acetylide and H₂.

q: The colours of the precipitates that ethyne gives with ammoniacal silver nitrate and with ammoniacal copper(I) chloride are, respectively:
x: Silver acetylide, Ag₂C₂, is a white precipitate; copper(I) acetylide, Cu₂C₂, is red (reddish-brown). Both tests show an acidic terminal hydrogen.

q: Ethyne reacts with sodamide, NaNH₂. The products are:
x: The strong base NH₂⁻ removes the acidic H⁺ from ethyne: HC≡CH + NaNH₂ → HC≡CNa + NH₃.

q: Sodium acetylide reacts with water to give back ethyne and sodium hydroxide. This shows that:
o: Ethyne is a stronger acid than water
Water is a weaker acid than ethane
Water is a stronger acid than ethyne
x: The acetylide ion takes H⁺ from water, so water gives up its proton more easily than ethyne does. Ethyne is only a very weak acid.

q: 5.2 g of ethyne reacts completely with ammoniacal copper(I) chloride to form copper(I) acetylide, Cu₂C₂. What mass of precipitate is formed? (C 12, H 1, Cu 63.5)
When ethyne loses H⁺ from one carbon, the anion HC≡C⁻ that is formed is called the:
x: Salts of this anion, such as sodium acetylide, are called acetylides. Ethoxide is C₂H₅O⁻, from ethanol.

q: Silver acetylide is warmed with dilute nitric acid. What happens?
o: Silver acetylide dissolves to give ethanal
x: The acid supplies H⁺ to the acetylide ion, giving back ethyne: Ag₂C₂ + 2HNO₃ → C₂H₂ + 2AgNO₃. This can be used to recover pure ethyne.

q: Ethyne is hydrated by passing it into dilute sulphuric acid. The catalyst used is:
x: Hydration of ethyne needs dilute H₂SO₄ with HgSO₄ (mercuric sulphate) as catalyst. Nickel is used for hydrogenation.

q: Ethyne is reacted with one mole of hydrogen using Lindlar's catalyst. The product is:
x: Lindlar's catalyst is a poisoned palladium catalyst that stops hydrogenation at the alkene stage.

q: Propyne reacts with excess hydrogen bromide (two moles). The final product is:
x: Each addition follows Markovnikov's rule: H goes to the carbon with more hydrogens and Br to C2. The first addition gives 2-bromopropene, the second puts another Br on C2.

q: But-1-yne, CH≡CCH₂CH₃, is hydrated with dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄. The final product is:
x: Water adds by Markovnikov's rule to give an enol with –OH on C2, which rearranges to the ketone CH₃COCH₂CH₃ (butanone). Only ethyne gives an aldehyde.

q: Ethyne reacts with one mole of hydrogen chloride. The product, used to make PVC, is:
x: One HCl adds across the triple bond to give CH₂=CHCl, chloroethene, whose polymer is polyvinyl chloride.

q: How many moles of hydrogen are needed to hydrogenate one mole of but-1-en-3-yne, CH₂=CH–C≡CH, completely to butane?
x: The C=C bond needs 1 mol H₂ and the C≡C bond needs 2 mol H₂, a total of 3 mol.

q: 13 g of ethyne is hydrated completely with dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄. What mass of ethanal, CH₃CHO, is formed? (C 12, H 1, O 16)
x: Moles of C₂H₂ = 13/26 = 0.5. One mole gives one mole of CH₃CHO (M = 44), so mass = 0.5 × 44 = 22 g.

q: In an addition reaction, two reactant molecules:
o: Exchange atoms to form two products
Each split into two smaller molecules
Combine to form a single product
Lose a small molecule such as water
x: In addition, atoms add across a multiple bond and one product results, e.g. C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂. Losing a small molecule describes elimination.

q: The reaction C₂H₅Br + KOH(aq) → C₂H₅OH + KBr is classified as:
x: The –OH group replaces the bromine atom on the same carbon, so it is a (nucleophilic) substitution. With alcoholic KOH, elimination to ethene would occur instead.

q: How does the number of π bonds in the organic reactant change in addition and in substitution reactions?
o: It increases in addition but decreases in substitution
It stays the same in addition but decreases in substitution
It decreases in both types of reaction
It decreases in addition but stays the same in substitution
x: Addition uses π bonds to form new σ bonds, so unsaturation falls. In substitution one atom or group simply replaces another, so the number of π bonds does not change.

q: The nitration of benzene, C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O (with concentrated H₂SO₄), is an example of:
x: The electrophile NO₂⁺ replaces one ring hydrogen, and the aromatic ring is kept, so it is electrophilic substitution.

q: The reaction HC≡CH + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₃ (over heated nickel) is an example of:
x: Hydrogen atoms add across the triple bond and no atom is replaced, so the reaction is addition (hydrogenation).

q: Which of the following is a substitution reaction?
o: Methylbenzene with chlorine in bright sunlight at its boiling point
Benzene with hydrogen over heated nickel
x: In sunlight, chlorine replaces a hydrogen of the –CH₃ side chain to give C₆H₅CH₂Cl and HCl. The other three reactions add atoms across multiple bonds.

q: Hydrocarbon P reacts with Br₂ to give C₂H₄Br₂ as the only product. Hydrocarbon Q reacts with Br₂ in sunlight to give C₂H₅Br and HBr. Which statement is correct?
o: P is ethane and reacts by substitution; Q is ethene and reacts by addition
P is ethene and reacts by addition; Q is ethane and reacts by substitution
Both are ethene and react by addition
P is ethyne and reacts by substitution; Q is ethene and reacts by addition
x: Ethene adds Br₂ across C=C with no by-product. Ethane has no π bond, so in light a Br atom replaces an H atom, releasing HBr.
